newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's PM Prodi faces committal hearing this week.
newsitem.headline: Italy's PM Prodi faces committal hearing this week.

text.p: A prosecutor's bid to try Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi for alleged abuse of office and conflict of interest could face its first test this week.
A committal hearing is scheduled in Rome on Wednesday to examine the request, which relates to events in 1993 when Prodi was chairman of the huge state holding group IRI.
As is often the case in Italy's slow-moving judicial system, the closed-door hearing is likely to open on Wednesday and then immediately be adjourned to a later date.
This is because a lawyer representing another defendant in the case has already told the court he cannot attend because he is required at a trial in the northern city of Turin.

That trial involves another giant in Italian life, Cesare Romiti, chairman of carmaker Fiat. Romiti goes on trial with Fiat finance director Francesco Paolo Mattioli on charges of accounting and tax fraud and making illegal payments.
The examining judge hearing Prodi's case, Eduardo Landi, must decide whether there is enough evidence to charge Prodi and five other former IRI directors and order a trial.
He also could dismiss the case or send it back to prosecutors for further investigation.
Prodi, who has headed a centre-left coalition since last May, has denied wrongdoing and said he was not even contemplating resignation.

Sergio Romano, a prominent political commentator, said the political fallout from the case had been negligible, especially when compared to public outrage stirred by the corruption cases of the early 1990s which toppled Italy's old political class.
"He feels confident he has nothing to do with it and his own statement, 'I will not step down', was not questioned by his allies," Romano said in a telephone interview.
"I don't think there will be a major shake-up," he said.

Prodi and the five other defendants have been accused of complicity in abuse of office for a sale by IRI in October 1993 of the food company Cirio, best known for its canned tomatoes, to a little-known southern Italian consortium, Fis.Vi.
Rome prosecutor Giuseppa Geremia alleges IRI's board gave the buyer an "unjust advantage" in the sale.
Fis.Vi soon after sold the food company's olive oil interests to the Anglo-Dutch group Unilever, for which Prodi had recently worked as a consultant.
Prodi denies his relationship with Unilever held any conflict of interest, saying he had cut his ties with the group months earlier, in May 1993, when he became chairman of IRI.
Prodi's main political rival, opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi, has been particularly quiet about the prime minister's legal problems.
Berlusconi had a similar experience when he was prime minister in 1994 and prosecutors in Milan brought corruption charges against him relating to his media empire.
He resigned a month later, in December 1994, when one of the parties in his centre-right coalition withdrew support, but remains opposition leader despite his trial.
